prompt: A café owner is planning next month. Does each decision set a price, which produces revenue, or is it another element of the mix, which represents a cost?

cards.text: Setting the price of a large latte at $5.25
cards.explanation: This is a price. Price is the only element in the marketing mix that produces revenue.

cards.text: Adding an oat-milk option to the menu
cards.explanation: A new menu option is part of the product, and it represents a cost to the café.

cards.text: Signing up with a delivery app
cards.explanation: Delivery is a channel decision. It represents a cost, not revenue.

cards.text: Raising the price of croissants from $3.50 to $3.75
cards.explanation: A price change produces revenue, and it can be made quickly, by the next morning.
This is promotion. All other elements represent costs to the organization.

cards.text: Charging $1 for an extra espresso shot
cards.explanation: It sets what customers pay, so it is price, the element that produces revenue.

cards.text: Printing new cups with the café's logo
cards.explanation: New cups are part of the product the café offers. They cost money to make.

prompt: A small roaster in Verdun is pricing a bag of coffee. Does each fact help set the lower limit on price, or the upper limit?

cards.text: Green beans cost $9 for each bag roasted
cards.explanation: This is a variable cost. Costs set the lower limit for price.

cards.text: Shoppers say they would not pay more than $24 a bag
cards.explanation: What buyers will pay is the market. The market sets the upper limit.

cards.text: Rent on the roastery is $3,000 a month
cards.explanation: Rent is a fixed cost. Total costs must be covered, so costs set the floor.

cards.text: At $22 a bag, far fewer shoppers buy than at $18
cards.explanation: This is the relationship between price and demand, which comes from the market.

cards.text: Paying the roaster for each hour of roasting
cards.explanation: Labour that grows with production is a variable cost, part of the lower limit.

cards.text: Many other roasters sell similar bags nearby
cards.explanation: Competitive conditions are part of the market, which limits how high the price can go.

question_text: Before designing a new e-bike, a Montréal company asks riders what they value and what that is worth to them. It then sets a target price and designs the bike to meet it. Which approach is this?
hint: The company started with the buyers, not with its costs.

options.option_explanation: Cost-based pricing starts from the product and its costs. This company started with what riders value.
Correct. The company assesses customer needs and value perceptions first, and uses them as the key to pricing.
Competition-based pricing looks at competitors' strategies, prices, costs, and offerings. This company asked riders.
Current profit maximization is a marketing objective. The question asks which pricing approach the company used.

prompt: Which pricing approach is each business using?

cases.text: A bakery adds up flour, labour, and delivery for each cake, then adds 20% on top.
cases.explanation: The price starts from the costs of producing, distributing, and selling, plus a return.

cases.text: A gas station checks the price at the station across the street every morning and sets its own to match.
cases.explanation: The price is set from what competitors charge.

cases.text: A theatre company asks its audience what an evening out is worth to them before it sets ticket prices.
cases.explanation: It assesses customer needs and value perceptions first, then sets the price.

cases.text: A new gym in Laval compares its hours and equipment with nearby gyms, finds it offers more, and prices above them.
cases.explanation: It compared its offer with competitors. Greater value justified a higher price.

cases.text: A furniture maker prices each chair to cover what it costs to make, ship, and sell, plus a fair return.
cases.explanation: Costs plus a fair rate of return for effort and risk: cost-based pricing.

cases.text: Before building a budgeting app, a start-up asks students what features they need and what those are worth to them.
cases.explanation: Buyers' perceptions of value are the key to the price, set before the product is built.

question_text: A company plans to launch a new product with market-skimming pricing. Which situation would make that plan a poor choice?
hint: Look at what must be true for a high price to hold.

options.option_text: Its quality and image support a high price
options.option_explanation: Product quality and image must support the high price, so this helps skimming.

options.option_text: Rivals could easily enter and undercut it
options.option_explanation: Correct. Competitors should not be able to easily enter the market and undercut the high price.

options.option_text: It expects fewer but more profitable sales
options.option_explanation: That is what skimming is meant to produce: fewer but more profitable sales.

options.option_text: It will skim revenues layer by layer
options.option_explanation: Skimming maximum revenues layer by layer is the definition of the strategy, not a problem with it.

prompt: Which product mix pricing strategy is each company using?

cases.text: A printer maker sells its printers cheaply and earns most of its profit on ink cartridges that only fit them.
cases.explanation: The cartridges must be used with the printer, and they carry the high markups.

cases.text: A car dealer sells the base model and lets buyers add heated seats and a sunroof for extra.
cases.explanation: The extras are optional products priced along with the main product.

cases.text: A hotel sells standard rooms at $150, deluxe rooms at $210, and suites at $340.
cases.explanation: It sets the price steps between the products in one line.

cases.text: An electric toothbrush sells for $30, and its replacement brush heads only fit that brush.
cases.explanation: The heads must be used with the main product, so they are captive products.

cases.text: A pizzeria charges extra for each topping a customer adds to a cheese pizza.
cases.explanation: It decides what is in the base price and what is offered as an option.

cases.text: A phone maker prices its three models $200 apart, based on their features and rivals' prices.
cases.explanation: Price steps based on feature evaluations and competitors' prices: product line pricing.
